title: Neuromorphic Event-Camera Imaging and Image Reconstruction
content: Event cameras, also known as dynamic vision sensors, depart from the synchronous frame-based imaging paradigm by reporting per-pixel brightness changes asynchronously as a stream of events. Each event encodes a pixel coordinate, a microsecond-resolution timestamp, and the polarity of a logarithmic-intensity change that has crossed a contrast threshold. This principle yields microsecond temporal resolution, a dynamic range exceeding $120$~dB, sparse output, and very low power, making event cameras attractive for high-speed and high-dynamic-range scenarios in which conventional cameras suffer from motion blur and saturation. However, the sparse asynchronous nature of events is incompatible with the dense tensor inputs expected by mainstream computer-vision pipelines, motivating the long-standing problem of reconstructing intensity images and video from event streams. In this paper we review the operating principles of the principal event-sensor families, survey the literature on event-based vision and intensity reconstruction, and present a recurrent encoder--decoder network that converts spatiotemporal event tensors into grayscale frames. We formalize the logarithmic event-generation model, define a composite objective combining per-pixel fidelity, perceptual, and temporal-consistency terms, and describe training and inference in an algorithm block. We report illustrative results on standard reconstruction-quality metrics, namely PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, together with high-dynamic-range and high-speed scenarios.
